task: Choose the correct option: My train gets in at six. ___, I'll call you from the station.
correct answer: When I arrive
wrong options / checks: If I arrive | When I will arrive | If I will arrive
explanation shown to learner: The train time is fixed, so the arrival is sure: *when*. After *when*, the present simple: *When I arrive*, not *When I will arrive*.
explanation in Latvian: *Vilciena* laiks ir zināms, tātad ierašanās ir droša: *when*. Aiz *when* lieto Present Simple: *When I arrive*, nevis *When I will arrive.*

task: Choose the correct option: I may not get the job, but ___, I'll move to Oslo.
correct answer: if I get it
wrong options / checks: when I get it | if I'll get it | when I'll get it
explanation shown to learner: *I may not get the job*: it is not sure, so *if*. *when* would mean you are sure. After *if*, the present simple: *if I get it*.
explanation in Latvian: *I may not get the job*: tas nav droši, tāpēc *if*. *when* nozīmētu, ka esi drošs. Aiz *if* lieto Present Simple: *if I get it*.

task: Which sentence is correct?
correct answer: The film ends at nine, so I'll call you when it finishes.
wrong options / checks: The film ends at nine, so I'll call you if it finishes. | The film ends at nine, so I'll call you when it will finish. | The film ends at nine, so I'll call you if it will finish.
explanation shown to learner: The film surely ends, so *when*, and after *when* the present simple: *when it finishes*.
explanation in Latvian: Filma noteikti beigsies, tāpēc *when*, un aiz *when* lieto Present Simple: *when it finishes*.

task: Choose the correct option: My brother might visit us next month. ___, we'll take him to the new museum.
correct answer: If he comes
wrong options / checks: When he comes | If he will come | When he will come
explanation shown to learner: *might visit*: the visit is not sure, so *if*. After *if*, the present simple: *If he comes*.
explanation in Latvian: *might visit*: ciemošanās nav droša, tāpēc *if*. Aiz *if* lieto Present Simple: *If he comes.*

task: Which sentence is NOT correct?
correct answer: I'll text you when I will land in Riga.
wrong options / checks: If the weather is nice tomorrow, we'll go for a walk. | When I'm in London next week, I'll visit the new gallery. | If you need help with the move, just call me.
explanation shown to learner: After *when* and *if*, use the present simple for the future, not *will*: *when I land*, not *when I will land*.
explanation in Latvian: Tulkojot burtiski kad nolaidīšos, gribas lietot *will*. Angliski aiz *when* un *if* nākotnei lieto Present Simple: *when I land*.

task: Choose the correct option: We're getting married in June. ___ married, we'll look for a bigger flat.
correct answer: When we're
wrong options / checks: If we're | When we'll be | If we'll be
explanation shown to learner: The wedding is planned, so it is sure: *when*. After *when*, the present simple: *When we're married*, not *When we'll be married*.
explanation in Latvian: Kāzas ir ieplānotas, tātad tas ir droši: *when*. Aiz *when* lieto Present Simple: *When we're married*, nevis *When we'll be married.*

task: Choose the correct option: ___ my visa in time, I'll fly to Toronto in May. It's not certain yet.
correct answer: If I get
wrong options / checks: When I get | If I'll get | When I'll get
explanation shown to learner: *It's not certain yet*, so *if*. After *if*, the present simple: *If I get my visa*.
explanation in Latvian: *It's not certain yet*: tas vēl nav droši, tāpēc *if*. Aiz *if* lieto Present Simple: *If I get my visa.*

task: Write *if* or *when*: I'm having lunch with Tom today. ___ I see him, I'll give him your book.
correct answer: When
explanation shown to learner: Lunch with Tom is planned, so you are sure to see him: *when*.
explanation in Latvian: *Pusdienas* ar *Tomu* ir norunātas, tātad viņu noteikti satiksi: *when*.

task: When the update ___, the app will restart by itself. (finish)
correct answer: finishes | has finished | 's finished | is finished
explanation shown to learner: After *when*, the present simple (or the present perfect) for the future, not *will*: *When the update finishes*.
explanation in Latvian: Aiz *when* nākotnei lieto Present Simple (vai Present Perfect), nevis *will*: *When the update finishes.*

task: Write *if* or *when*: The bank might be closed on Saturday. ___ it is, I'll go on Monday.
correct answer: If
explanation shown to learner: *might be closed*: it is not sure, so *if*.
explanation in Latvian: *might be closed*: tas nav droši, tāpēc *if*.

task: My course starts on Monday. When it ___, I'll have less free time. (start)
correct answer: starts | has started | 's started
explanation shown to learner: After *when*, the present simple for the future: *When it starts*, not *When it will start*.
explanation in Latvian: Aiz *when* nākotnei lieto Present Simple: *When it starts*, nevis *When it will start.*

task: Write *if* or *when*: The museum opens at ten. ___ it opens, we'll buy tickets for the tower.
correct answer: When
explanation shown to learner: The opening time is fixed, so it is sure: *when*.
explanation in Latvian: Atvēršanas laiks ir zināms, tātad tas ir droši: *when*.

task: Join with *if* or *when*: My contract ends in June. Then I'll take a long holiday.
correct answer: When my contract ends in June, I'll take a long holiday. | When my contract ends in June, I will take a long holiday. | When my contract ends, I'll take a long holiday. | When my contract ends, I will take a long holiday. | I'll take a long holiday when my contract ends in June. | I will take a long holiday when my contract ends in June. | I'll take a long holiday when my contract ends. | I will take a long holiday when my contract ends. | In June, when my contract ends, I'll take a long holiday. | In June, when my contract ends, I will take a long holiday. | I'll take a long holiday in June, when my contract ends. | I will take a long holiday in June, when my contract ends. | When my contract has ended, I'll take a long holiday. | When my contract has ended, I will take a long holiday. | I'll take a long holiday when my contract has ended. | I will take a long holiday when my contract has ended.
explanation shown to learner: The contract surely ends in June, so *when*, and after *when* the present simple: *When my contract ends*.
explanation in Latvian: Līgums jūnijā noteikti beigsies, tāpēc *when*, un aiz *when* lieto Present Simple: *When my contract ends.*

task: Join with *if* or *when*: Perhaps the hotel is full. In that case, we'll stay with friends.
correct answer: If the hotel is full, we'll stay with friends. | If the hotel is full, we will stay with friends. | If the hotel's full, we'll stay with friends. | If the hotel's full, we will stay with friends. | We'll stay with friends if the hotel is full. | We will stay with friends if the hotel is full. | We'll stay with friends if the hotel's full. | We will stay with friends if the hotel's full. | If the hotel is full, then we'll stay with friends. | If the hotel is full, we'll stay with friends instead. | We'll stay with friends instead if the hotel is full.
explanation shown to learner: *Perhaps*: it is not sure, so *if*, with the present simple: *If the hotel is full*.
explanation in Latvian: *Perhaps*: tas nav droši, tāpēc *if* un Present Simple: *If the hotel is full.*

task: Join with *when*: I'll finish this email. Then I'll call you back.
correct answer: When I finish this email, I'll call you back. | When I finish this email, I will call you back. | When I've finished this email, I'll call you back. | When I've finished this email, I will call you back. | When I have finished this email, I'll call you back. | When I have finished this email, I will call you back. | I'll call you back when I finish this email. | I will call you back when I finish this email. | I'll call you back when I've finished this email. | I will call you back when I've finished this email. | I'll call you back when I have finished this email. | I will call you back when I have finished this email.
explanation shown to learner: After *when*, the present simple (or the present perfect) for the future, not *will*: *When I finish this email*.
explanation in Latvian: Aiz *when* nākotnei lieto Present Simple (vai Present Perfect), nevis *will*: *When I finish this email.*

task: Put the words in order to make a question.
correct answer: what will you do when you finish your degree
wrong options / checks: also accepted: when you finish your degree what will you do
explanation shown to learner: In the question *will* goes before *you*; the *when*-part keeps the present simple and can come first or second.
explanation in Latvian: Jautājumā *will* stāv pirms *you*. Daļā ar *when* paliek Present Simple, un tā var būt pirmā vai otrā.

task: Put the words in order to make a question.
correct answer: will you text me when your plane lands in rome
wrong options / checks: also accepted: when your plane lands in rome will you text me
explanation shown to learner: In the question *will* goes before *you*; the *when*-part keeps the present simple and can come first or second.
explanation in Latvian: Jautājumā *will* stāv pirms *you*. Daļā ar *when* paliek Present Simple, un tā var būt pirmā vai otrā.

task: Put the words in order.
correct answer: if the meeting finishes early i'll go to the gym
wrong options / checks: also accepted: i'll go to the gym if the meeting finishes early
explanation shown to learner: *if* + present simple, *will* in the other part. The *if*-part can come first (with a comma) or second.
explanation in Latvian: *if* + Present Simple, *will* otrā daļā. *if* daļa var būt pirmā (ar komatu) vai otrā.

task: Put the words in order.
correct answer: i'll send you the photos of the flat when i get home
wrong options / checks: also accepted: when i get home i'll send you the photos of the flat
explanation shown to learner: *when* + present simple, *will* in the other part. The *when*-part can come first (with a comma) or second.
explanation in Latvian: *when* + Present Simple, *will* otrā daļā. *when* daļa var būt pirmā (ar komatu) vai otrā.

task: Put the words in order.
correct answer: my parents will move to the coast when they retire
wrong options / checks: also accepted: when they retire my parents will move to the coast | when my parents retire they will move to the coast
explanation shown to learner: *when* + present simple, *will* in the other part. The *when*-part can come first (with a comma) or second.
explanation in Latvian: *when* + Present Simple, *will* otrā daļā. *when* daļa var būt pirmā (ar komatu) vai otrā.

task: My new laptop arrives on Friday. ___ it ___, I'll set it up for you.
correct answer: When / arrives
wrong options / checks: bank: When | If | arrives | will arrive
explanation shown to learner: The delivery day is fixed, so it is sure: *when*. After *when*, the present simple: *When it arrives*.
explanation in Latvian: Piegādes diena ir zināma, tātad tas ir droši: *when*. Aiz *when* lieto Present Simple: *When it arrives.*

task: I might not finish the report today. ___ I ___ it, I'll send it to you tonight.
correct answer: If / finish
wrong options / checks: bank: If | When | finish | will finish
explanation shown to learner: *might not finish*: it is not sure, so *if*. After *if*, the present simple: *If I finish it*.
explanation in Latvian: *might not finish*: tas nav droši, tāpēc *if*. Aiz *if* lieto Present Simple: *If I finish it.*

task: We're moving to Riga in March. ___ there, we'll see each other more often.
correct answer: When we're
wrong options / checks: bank: When we're | If we're | When we'll be
explanation shown to learner: The move is planned, so it is sure: *when*, with the present simple: *When we're there*.
explanation in Latvian: Pārcelšanās ir ieplānota, tātad tas ir droši: *when* un Present Simple: *When we're there.*

task: I might get tickets for the concert. ___ I ___ them, I'll take you with me.
correct answer: If / get
wrong options / checks: bank: If | When | get | will get
explanation shown to learner: *might get*: it is not sure, so *if*. After *if*, the present simple: *If I get them*.
explanation in Latvian: *might get*: tas nav droši, tāpēc *if*. Aiz *if* lieto Present Simple: *If I get them.*

task: Match each sentence with the one that follows it.
correct answer: My flight lands at six. = When it does, I'll text you. ; My flight might be late. = If it is, I'll take a taxi. ; I'm not sure the hotel has parking. = If it doesn't, we'll park at the station. ; Our room will be ready at two. = When it is, we'll take our bags up.
explanation shown to learner: Something sure (*lands at six*, *will be ready*) takes *when*; something not sure (*might*, *not sure*) takes *if*.
explanation in Latvian: Drošam notikumam (*lands at six, will be ready*) lieto *when*; nedrošam (*might, not sure*) lieto *if*.

task: Choose the correct option: My laptop is eight years old, but it continues ___ without any problems.
correct answer: to work
wrong options / checks: work | to working
explanation shown to learner: After *continue* use *-ing* or *to* + base verb: *it continues to work* (*it continues working* is correct too). Not *it continues work / to working*.
explanation in Latvian: Aiz *continue* lieto formu ar *-ing* vai to + pamatformu: *it continues to work* (der arī *it continues working*). Nevis *it continues work / to working*.

task: Choose the correct option: When the band came on stage, the whole crowd started ___.
correct answer: dancing
wrong options / checks: dance | danced | to dancing
explanation shown to learner: After *start* use *-ing* or *to* + base verb: *the crowd started dancing* (*started to dance* is correct too). Not *started dance / danced / to dancing*.
explanation in Latvian: Aiz *start* lieto formu ar *-ing* vai to + pamatformu: *the crowd started dancing* (der arī *started to dance*). Nevis *started dance / danced / to dancing*.

task: Which sentence is NOT correct?
correct answer: I'd like going to the concert with you on Saturday.
wrong options / checks: My sister hates to fly, so she always takes the train. | We started building our new website in January. | He continued to work part-time after he retired.
explanation shown to learner: *would like* takes only *to*: *I'd like to go to the concert.* After *hate, start, continue* both forms are correct (*hates flying / hates to fly*).
explanation in Latvian: *would like* lieto tikai ar *to*: *I'd like to go to the concert.* Aiz *hate, start, continue* der abas formas (*hates flying / hates to fly*).

task: Choose the correct option: We'd love ___ to your party, but we're away that weekend.
correct answer: to come
wrong options / checks: coming | come | to coming
explanation shown to learner: *would like / would love / would prefer* + *to* + base verb, never *-ing*: *We'd love to come.* Not *We'd love coming / come / to coming*.
explanation in Latvian: *would like / would love / would prefer + to* + pamatforma, nekad ar *-ing*: *We'd love to come.* Nevis *We'd love coming / come / to coming.*

task: Which sentence is NOT correct?
correct answer: She started learn Spanish when she moved to Valencia.
wrong options / checks: I love cooking for my friends at the weekend. | They began to argue as soon as the meeting started. | Would you prefer to sit by the window?
explanation shown to learner: After *start* use *-ing* or *to* + base verb: *She started learning / to learn Spanish.* The base form alone is wrong.
explanation in Latvian: Aiz *start* lieto formu ar *-ing* vai to + pamatformu: *She started learning / to learn Spanish.* Tikai pamatforma ir kļūda. Tulkojot burtiski "sāka mācīties", sanāk *started learn*.

task: Which sentence is correct?
correct answer: My husband hates driving at night, so I usually drive us home.
wrong options / checks: My husband hates drive at night, so I usually drive us home. | My husband hates to driving at night, so I usually drive us home.
explanation shown to learner: After *hate* use *-ing* or *to* + base verb: *hates driving* or *hates to drive*. Not the base form alone, and not *to* + *-ing*.
explanation in Latvian: Aiz *hate* lieto formu ar *-ing* vai to + pamatformu: *hates driving* vai *hates to drive*. Nevis tikai pamatformu un nevis *to + -ing*.

task: Which sentence is NOT correct?
correct answer: We like eat out on Friday evenings after a long week.
wrong options / checks: Our team began to use the new software last month. | She prefers to cycle to work when the weather is nice. | Would you like to join our book club this autumn?
explanation shown to learner: After *like* use *-ing* or *to* + base verb: *We like eating out / We like to eat out.* The base form alone is wrong.
explanation in Latvian: Aiz *like* lieto formu ar *-ing* vai to + pamatformu: *We like eating out / We like to eat out.* Tikai pamatforma ir kļūda. Tulkojot burtiski "mums patīk ēst ārpus mājas", sanāk *we like eat out*.

task: The audience began ___ before the actor finished his joke. (laugh)
correct answer: laughing | to laugh
explanation shown to learner: After *begin* both forms are correct, with the same meaning: *began laughing* = *began to laugh*.
explanation in Latvian: Aiz *begin* der abas formas, ar *-ing* un ar to + pamatformu, un nozīme ir tā pati: *began laughing = began to laugh*.

task: My partner loves ___ new recipes, so we often have friends over at the weekend. (try)
correct answer: trying | to try
explanation shown to learner: After *love* both forms are correct, with the same meaning: *loves trying* = *loves to try*.
explanation in Latvian: Aiz *love* der abas formas, ar *-ing* un ar to + pamatformu, un nozīme ir tā pati: *loves trying = loves to try*.

task: Do you prefer ___ on holiday alone or with friends? (go)
correct answer: going | to go
explanation shown to learner: After *prefer* both forms are correct, with the same meaning: *Do you prefer going* = *Do you prefer to go*.
explanation in Latvian: Aiz *prefer* der abas formas, ar *-ing* un ar to + pamatformu, un nozīme ir tā pati: *Do you prefer going = Do you prefer to go.*

task: Many people continued ___ from home after the offices reopened. (work)
correct answer: working | to work
explanation shown to learner: After *continue* both forms are correct, with the same meaning: *continued working* = *continued to work*.
explanation in Latvian: Aiz *continue* der abas formas, ar *-ing* un ar to + pamatformu, un nozīme ir tā pati: *continued working = continued to work*.

task: I hate ___ on the phone, so I usually send a text message instead. (talk)
correct answer: talking | to talk
explanation shown to learner: After *hate* both forms are correct, with the same meaning: *I hate talking* = *I hate to talk*.
explanation in Latvian: Aiz *hate* der abas formas, ar *-ing* un ar to + pamatformu, un nozīme ir tā pati: *I hate talking = I hate to talk.*

task: Say it another way with *to*: We started looking for a new flat as soon as I got the job.
correct answer: We started to look for a new flat as soon as I got the job. | As soon as I got the job, we started to look for a new flat.
explanation shown to learner: After *start* both forms are correct, with the same meaning: *started looking* = *started to look*.
explanation in Latvian: Aiz *start* der abas formas, ar *-ing* un ar to + pamatformu, un nozīme ir tā pati: *started looking = started to look*.

task: Correct the mistake: I love spend time with my cousins because they always make me laugh.
correct answer: I love spending time with my cousins because they always make me laugh. | I love to spend time with my cousins because they always make me laugh.
explanation shown to learner: After *love* use *-ing* or *to* + base verb, both are correct: *I love spending time* = *I love to spend time*. The base form alone is wrong.
explanation in Latvian: Aiz *love* lieto formu ar *-ing* vai to + pamatformu, abas ir pareizas: *I love spending time = I love to spend time.* Tikai pamatforma ir kļūda.

task: Correct the mistake: Would you like coming with us to the team lunch on Friday?
correct answer: Would you like to come with us to the team lunch on Friday?
explanation shown to learner: *would like / would love / would prefer* + *to* + base verb, never *-ing*: *Would you like to come with us?* Not *Would you like coming*.
explanation in Latvian: *would like / would love / would prefer + to* + pamatforma, nekad ar *-ing*: *Would you like to come with us?* Nevis *Would you like coming.*

task: Put the words in order.
correct answer: she began to write a blog about her travels last year
wrong options / checks: also accepted: last year she began to write a blog about her travels
explanation shown to learner: After *begin* both forms are correct, with the same meaning: *began to write* = *began writing*.
explanation in Latvian: Aiz *begin* der abas formas, ar *-ing* un ar to + pamatformu, un nozīme ir tā pati: *began to write = began writing*.

task: Put the words in order to make a question.
correct answer: would you like to have a coffee before the meeting
explanation shown to learner: *would like / would love / would prefer* + *to* + base verb, never *-ing*: *Would you like to have a coffee?* Not *Would you like having*. In a question the helping verb (or *am / is / are*) goes before the subject.
explanation in Latvian: *would like / would love / would prefer + to* + pamatforma, nekad ar *-ing*: *Would you like to have a coffee?* Nevis *Would you like having.* Jautājumā palīgdarbības vārds (vai *am / is / are*) stāv pirms teikuma priekšmeta.

task: Put the words in order.
correct answer: my father started using a smartphone when he turned seventy
wrong options / checks: also accepted: when he turned seventy my father started using a smartphone | when my father turned seventy he started using a smartphone
explanation shown to learner: After *start* both forms are correct, with the same meaning: *started using* = *started to use*.
explanation in Latvian: Aiz *start* der abas formas, ar *-ing* un ar to + pamatformu, un nozīme ir tā pati: *started using = started to use*.

task: Put the words in order.
correct answer: she continued working at the hospital after her first child was born
wrong options / checks: also accepted: after her first child was born she continued working at the hospital
explanation shown to learner: After *continue* both forms are correct, with the same meaning: *continued working* = *continued to work*.
explanation in Latvian: Aiz *continue* der abas formas, ar *-ing* un ar to + pamatformu, un nozīme ir tā pati: *continued working = continued to work*.

task: Put the words in order to make a question.
correct answer: do you prefer to cook at home or go to restaurants
wrong options / checks: also accepted: do you prefer to go to restaurants or cook at home
explanation shown to learner: After *prefer* both forms are correct, with the same meaning: *prefer to cook* = *prefer cooking*. In a question the helping verb (or *am / is / are*) goes before the subject.
explanation in Latvian: Aiz *prefer* der abas formas, ar *-ing* un ar to + pamatformu, un nozīme ir tā pati: *prefer to cook = prefer cooking*. Jautājumā palīgdarbības vārds (vai *am / is / are*) stāv pirms teikuma priekšmeta.

task: During the long winter my brother started ___ his own furniture, and now he sells it online.
correct answer: making
wrong options / checks: bank: making | make | to making
explanation shown to learner: After *start* use *-ing* or *to* + base verb: *he started making* (*he started to make* is correct too). Not *started make / to making*.
explanation in Latvian: Aiz *start* lieto formu ar *-ing* vai to + pamatformu: *he started making* (der arī *he started to make*). Nevis *started make / to making*.

task: I'd like ___ a table for four at eight o'clock, please.
correct answer: to book
wrong options / checks: bank: to book | booking | book
explanation shown to learner: *would like / would love / would prefer* + *to* + base verb, never *-ing*: *I'd like to book a table.* Not *I'd like booking / book*.
explanation in Latvian: *would like / would love / would prefer + to* + pamatforma, nekad ar *-ing*: *I'd like to book a table.* Nevis *I'd like booking / book.*

task: My parents love ___ in the mountains, so they go there every summer.
correct answer: walking
wrong options / checks: bank: walking | walk | to walking
explanation shown to learner: After *love* use *-ing* or *to* + base verb: *they love walking* (*they love to walk* is correct too). Not *love walk / to walking*.
explanation in Latvian: Aiz *love* lieto formu ar *-ing* vai to + pamatformu: *they love walking* (der arī *they love to walk*). Nevis *love walk / to walking*.

task: House prices will probably continue ___ next year, so this is a good time to buy.
correct answer: to rise
wrong options / checks: bank: to rise | rise | to rising
explanation shown to learner: After *continue* use *-ing* or *to* + base verb: *prices will continue to rise* (*continue rising* is correct too). Not *continue rise / to rising*.
explanation in Latvian: Aiz *continue* lieto formu ar *-ing* vai to + pamatformu: *prices will continue to rise* (der arī *continue rising*). Nevis *continue rise / to rising*.

task: Match each beginning with its ending.
correct answer: We left the beach early because it started = raining just after lunch. ; The baby on the plane woke up and began = to cry loudly. ; My grandmother is 85, but she still loves = working in her garden every day. ; When you're back, I'd love = to see the photos from your trip.
explanation shown to learner: After *start, begin, love* both *-ing* and *to* + verb are correct (*started raining = started to rain*). *would love* takes only *to*: *I'd love to see the photos.*
explanation in Latvian: Aiz *start, begin, love* der abas formas (*started raining = started to rain*). *would love* lieto tikai ar *to*: *I'd love to see the photos.*

task: Choose the correct option: The hotel was nice, but there was ___ hot water in our room.
correct answer: no
wrong options / checks: none | any | none of
explanation shown to learner: *was* is positive and a noun follows, so use *no*: *there was no hot water*. *none* is used without a noun.
explanation in Latvian: *was* nav noliegumā, un aiz tukšās vietas ir lietvārds: *there was no hot water*. *none* lieto bez lietvārda.

task: Choose the correct option: I needed paper for the printer, but there was ___ left.
correct answer: none
wrong options / checks: no | any | none of
explanation shown to learner: *none* stands alone, without a noun: *There was none left.* Before a noun use *no*: *There was no bread.*
explanation in Latvian: *none* lieto bez lietvārda: *There was none left.* Ar lietvārdu: *There was no bread.*

task: Which sentence is correct?
correct answer: There aren't any shops in our village, so we drive to town.
wrong options / checks: There aren't no shops in our village, so we drive to town. | There are any shops in our village, so we drive to town. | There are none shops in our village, so we drive to town.
explanation shown to learner: Only one negative: *There isn't any milk* or *There's no milk*, not *There isn't no milk*.
explanation in Latvian: Tulkojot burtiski Nav nekāda piena, sanāk divi noliegumi (*There isn't no milk*). Angliski lieto tikai vienu: *There isn't any milk* vai *There's no milk.*

task: Which sentence is correct?
correct answer: None of my friends could come to my party, so I cancelled it.
wrong options / checks: No of my friends could come to my party, so I cancelled it. | None my friends could come to my party, so I cancelled it. | None of my friends couldn't come to my party, so I cancelled it.
explanation shown to learner: *None of* + *my friends*, and the verb stays positive: *None of my friends could come.* *None ... couldn't* is a double negative.
explanation in Latvian: *None of + my friends*, un darbības vārds nav noliegumā: *None of my friends could come.* *None* ... *couldn't* ir divi noliegumi.

task: Which sentence is NOT correct?
correct answer: I don't have nothing to wear to my cousin's wedding.
wrong options / checks: There's no time to cook tonight, so let's order a pizza. | None of the shops opened before ten on Sunday. | I haven't got any cash, so can I pay by card?
explanation shown to learner: Only one negative: *I don't have anything to wear* or *I have nothing to wear*, not *don't ... nothing*.
explanation in Latvian: Tulkojot burtiski Man nav nekā, ko vilkt, sanāk divi noliegumi. Angliski lieto vienu: *I don't have anything to wear* vai *I have nothing to wear.*

task: Choose the correct option: 'How many tickets are left for tonight's concert?' '___. They're all sold out.'
correct answer: None
wrong options / checks: No | Any | No one
explanation shown to learner: A short answer without a noun is *None*: *How many are left? None.* *No* needs a noun, and *no one* is for people.
explanation in Latvian: Īsa atbilde bez lietvārda ir *None*: *How many are left?* *None*. Ar lietvārdu saka no *tickets*, un no *one* attiecas uz cilvēkiem.

task: Choose the correct option: We asked five language schools about evening courses, but ___ them had a free place.
correct answer: none of
wrong options / checks: no | none | any of
explanation shown to learner: Before *the / my / them* use *none of*: *None of my friends came.* Not *No of*, not *None my friends*.
explanation in Latvian: Pirms *the / my / them* lieto *none of*: *None of my friends came.* Nevis No *of* un nevis *None my friends.*

task: Write *no* or *any*: My new phone has ___ headphone jack, so I use wireless earbuds.
correct answer: no
explanation shown to learner: *has* is positive, so use *no*: *It has no headphone jack.* (= *It doesn't have a headphone jack.*)
explanation in Latvian: *has* nav noliegumā: *It has no headphone jack.* (= *It doesn't have a headphone jack*.)

task: Write *no* or *any*: Our teacher didn't give us ___ homework over the holidays.
correct answer: any
explanation shown to learner: After a negative verb (*didn't, haven't, aren't*) use *any*, not *no*: *We haven't got any coffee.*
explanation in Latvian: Ja darbības vārds ir noliegumā (*didn't, haven't, aren't*), lieto *any*: *We haven't got any coffee*, nevis *haven't got no coffee*.

task: Write *no* or *none*: I wanted to buy fresh bread after work, but there was ___ left.
correct answer: none
explanation shown to learner: *none* stands alone, without a noun: *There was none left.* Before a noun use *no*: *There was no bread.*
explanation in Latvian: *none* lieto bez lietvārda: *There was none left.* Ar lietvārdu: *There was no bread.*

task: Write *no* or *none*: ___ of the photos I took at the concert came out well. It was too dark.
correct answer: None | none
explanation shown to learner: Before *the / my / them* use *none of*: *None of my friends came.* Not *No of*, not *None my friends*.
explanation in Latvian: Pirms *the / my / them* lieto *none of*: *None of my friends came.* Nevis No *of* un nevis *None my friends.*

task: Complete with one word: There ___ any direct flights, so we had to change planes in Frankfurt.
correct answer: weren't | aren't
explanation shown to learner: *any* goes with a negative verb: *There weren't any direct flights.* (= *There were no direct flights.*)
explanation in Latvian: *any* lieto ar darbības vārdu noliegumā: *There weren't any direct flights.* (= *There were no direct flights*.)

task: Say it another way with *no*: There aren't any vegetarian dishes on the menu.
correct answer: There are no vegetarian dishes on the menu. | On the menu there are no vegetarian dishes.
explanation shown to learner: *no* + noun = *not any* + noun: *There's no milk.* = *There isn't any milk.* The verb stays positive.
explanation in Latvian: *no milk = not any milk*: *There's no milk.* = *There isn't any milk.* Darbības vārds nav noliegumā.

task: Say it another way with *any*: I've got no plans for the weekend.
correct answer: I haven't got any plans for the weekend. | I don't have any plans for the weekend. | I've not got any plans for the weekend. | I haven't any plans for the weekend.
explanation shown to learner: After a negative verb (*didn't, haven't, aren't*) use *any*, not *no*: *We haven't got any coffee.*
explanation in Latvian: Ja darbības vārds ir noliegumā (*didn't, haven't, aren't*), lieto *any*: *We haven't got any coffee*, nevis *haven't got no coffee*.

task: Correct the mistake: We didn't get no answer from the bank, so I called them again.
correct answer: We didn't get any answer from the bank, so I called them again. | We got no answer from the bank, so I called them again. | We didn't get an answer from the bank, so I called them again.
explanation shown to learner: Only one negative: *We didn't get any answer* or *We got no answer*, not *didn't get no answer*.
explanation in Latvian: Tulkojot burtiski Mēs nesaņēmām nekādu atbildi, sanāk divi noliegumi. Angliski lieto vienu: *We didn't get any answer* vai *We got no answer.*

task: Put the words in order.
correct answer: i didn't have any time to revise for the test
explanation shown to learner: After a negative verb (*didn't, haven't, aren't*) use *any*, not *no*: *We haven't got any coffee.*
explanation in Latvian: Ja darbības vārds ir noliegumā (*didn't, haven't, aren't*), lieto *any*: *We haven't got any coffee*, nevis *haven't got no coffee*.

task: Put the words in order.
correct answer: none of my colleagues knew that the meeting was cancelled
explanation shown to learner: Before *the / my / them* use *none of*: *None of my friends came.* Not *No of*, not *None my friends*.
explanation in Latvian: Pirms *the / my / them* lieto *none of*: *None of my friends came.* Nevis No *of* un nevis *None my friends.*

task: Put the words in order to make a question.
correct answer: why are there no taxis at the station
explanation shown to learner: *no* + noun = *not any* + noun: *There's no milk.* = *There isn't any milk.* The verb stays positive. In a question the helping verb (or *am / is / are*) goes before the subject.
explanation in Latvian: *no milk = not any milk*: *There's no milk.* = *There isn't any milk.* Darbības vārds nav noliegumā. Jautājumā palīgdarbības vārds (vai *am / is / are*) stāv pirms teikuma priekšmeta.

task: Put the words in order.
correct answer: no cars are allowed in the old town at weekends
wrong options / checks: also accepted: at weekends no cars are allowed in the old town | in the old town no cars are allowed at weekends
explanation shown to learner: *no* + noun can start a sentence, and the verb stays positive: *No cars are allowed.*
explanation in Latvian: Teikums var sākties ar No *cars*, un darbības vārds nav noliegumā: *No cars are allowed.*

task: Put the words in order.
correct answer: we had no idea that they were getting married
explanation shown to learner: *no* + noun = *not any* + noun: *There's no milk.* = *There isn't any milk.* The verb stays positive.
explanation in Latvian: *no milk = not any milk*: *There's no milk.* = *There isn't any milk.* Darbības vārds nav noliegumā.

task: Sorry, there ___ ___ seats left on the morning train.
correct answer: are / no
wrong options / checks: bank: are | no | aren't | none
explanation shown to learner: Only one negative: *There isn't any milk* or *There's no milk*, not *There isn't no milk*.
explanation in Latvian: Tulkojot burtiski Nav nekāda piena, sanāk divi noliegumi (*There isn't no milk*). Angliski lieto tikai vienu: *There isn't any milk* vai *There's no milk.*

task: ___ ___ the students passed the first test, so the teacher explained it again.
correct answer: None / of
wrong options / checks: bank: None | of | No | Any
explanation shown to learner: Before *the / my / them* use *none of*: *None of my friends came.* Not *No of*, not *None my friends*.
explanation in Latvian: Pirms *the / my / them* lieto *none of*: *None of my friends came.* Nevis No *of* un nevis *None my friends.*

task: Our phones had ___ signal in the mountains, so we used a paper map.
correct answer: no
wrong options / checks: bank: no | any | none
explanation shown to learner: *no* + noun = *not any* + noun: *There's no milk.* = *There isn't any milk.* The verb stays positive.
explanation in Latvian: *no milk = not any milk*: *There's no milk.* = *There isn't any milk.* Darbības vārds nav noliegumā.

task: We haven't got ___ coffee left, so I'll buy some on the way home.
correct answer: any
wrong options / checks: bank: any | no | none
explanation shown to learner: After a negative verb (*didn't, haven't, aren't*) use *any*, not *no*: *We haven't got any coffee.*
explanation in Latvian: Ja darbības vārds ir noliegumā (*didn't, haven't, aren't*), lieto *any*: *We haven't got any coffee*, nevis *haven't got no coffee*.

task: Match each beginning with its ending.
correct answer: The hotel was full, so there were no = rooms for us. ; I sent my CV to four companies, but none of = them replied. ; I can't pay for the taxi. I don't have any = cash on me. ; I wanted more coffee, but there was = none left in the pot.
explanation shown to learner: *no* + noun (*no rooms*), *none of* + *them*, *not any* + noun (*don't have any cash*), *none* without a noun (*there was none left*).
explanation in Latvian: Ar lietvārdu: *there were no rooms* un *don't have any cash*; pirms *them*: *none of them*; bez lietvārda: *there was none left*.

task: Choose the correct option: My knee hurt so much last winter that I ___ stop running for two months.
correct answer: had to
wrong options / checks: must | have to | musted
explanation shown to learner: For the past use *had to*: *must* has no past form for obligation (not *must*, *have to* or *musted* with *last winter*).
explanation in Latvian: Pagātnē lieto *had to*: pienākumam *must* pagātnes formas nav (nevis *must, have to* vai *musted*, ja ir *last winter*).

task: Choose the correct option: The hotel is almost full, so we ___ find somewhere else to stay tonight.
correct answer: might have to
wrong options / checks: might must | might to | must have to
explanation shown to learner: *must* never follows another verb such as *might*, *will* or *going to*: use *have to* (*we might have to find …*, *we're going to have to …*).
explanation in Latvian: *must* nekad neliek aiz cita darbības vārda, piemēram, *might, will* vai *going to*: lieto *have to* (*we might have to find* …, *we're going to have to* …).

task: Which sentence is correct?
correct answer: Does your brother have to work late when the restaurant is busy?
wrong options / checks: Does your brother has to work late when the restaurant is busy? | Has your brother to work late when the restaurant is busy? | Do your brother have to work late when the restaurant is busy?
explanation shown to learner: Questions with *have to* use *do / does*: *Do I have to …? Does she have to …?* Not *Do I must*, *Have I to* or *Has she to*.
explanation in Latvian: Jautājumos ar *have to* lieto *do / does*: *Do I have to* …? *Does she have to* …? Nevis *Do I must, Have I to* vai *Has she to.*

task: Choose the correct option: ___ show my student card every time I use the library?
correct answer: Do I have to
wrong options / checks: Do I must | Have I to | Must I to
explanation shown to learner: Questions with *have to* use *do*: *Do I have to show …?* Not *Do I must* or *Have I to*, and no *to* after *must*.
explanation in Latvian: Jautājumos ar *have to* lieto *do*: *Do I have to show* …? Nevis *Do I must, Have I to* vai *Must I to.*

task: Choose the correct option: My manager ___ come to the office on Fridays, so she usually works from home.
correct answer: doesn't have to
wrong options / checks: hasn't to | don't have to | doesn't must
explanation shown to learner: *doesn't have to* = it is not necessary: *she doesn't have to come in*. With *he / she* use *doesn't*, not *don't*; *hasn't to* is not English.
explanation in Latvian: *doesn't have to* = nav vajadzības: *she doesn't have to come in*. Ar *he / she* lieto *doesn't*, nevis *don't*. *hasn't to* angliski nesaka.

task: Choose the correct option: These tablets can make you sleepy, so you ___ drive after taking them.
correct answer: mustn't
wrong options / checks: don't have to | don't must | mustn't to
explanation shown to learner: *mustn't* = it is not allowed, or it is important not to do it: the tablets make you sleepy. *don't have to* would mean it is not necessary.
explanation in Latvian: *mustn't* = nedrīkst: tabletes rada miegainību. *don't have to* nozīmētu, ka nav vajadzības. Tulkojot burtiski, *must not* šķiet 'nav jā…', bet 'nav jā…' ir *don't have to*.

task: Which sentence is NOT correct?
correct answer: From May, drivers will must pay to enter the city centre.
wrong options / checks: We had to wait an hour for a doctor at the clinic yesterday. | You might have to show your ID when you buy the tickets. | Do you have to pay for parking at your new office?
explanation shown to learner: *must* cannot follow *will*: use *will have to* (*we'll have to buy a new one*).
explanation in Latvian: Aiz *will* nevar likt *must*: lieto *will have to* (*we'll have to buy a new one*).

task: Which sentence is the speaker's own idea, not a rule?
correct answer: I must drink less coffee in the evenings.
wrong options / checks: Staff have to wear a badge in the building. | Passengers have to show their tickets on the train. | Students have to hand in the essay by Friday.
explanation shown to learner: In British English *must* often shows the speaker's own feeling (*I must drink less coffee*), *have to* a rule or a situation (*Staff have to wear a badge*). Very often both are possible.
explanation in Latvian: Britu angļu valodā *must* bieži izsaka paša runātāja sajūtu (*I must drink less coffee*), *have to* noteikumu vai situāciju (*Staff have to wear a badge*). Ļoti bieži der abi.

task: Put the words in order to make a question.
correct answer: do we have to print our boarding passes before we get to the airport
explanation shown to learner: Questions with *have to* use *do / does*: *Do I have to …? Does she have to …?* Not *Do I must*, *Have I to* or *Has she to*.
explanation in Latvian: Jautājumos ar *have to* lieto *do / does*: *Do I have to* …? *Does she have to* …? Nevis *Do I must, Have I to* vai *Has she to.*

task: Put the words in order to make a question.
correct answer: does the new manager have to speak latvian or is english enough
wrong options / checks: also accepted: does the new manager have to speak english or is latvian enough
explanation shown to learner: Questions with *have to* use *do / does*: *Do I have to …? Does she have to …?* Not *Do I must*, *Have I to* or *Has she to*.
explanation in Latvian: Jautājumos ar *have to* lieto *do / does*: *Do I have to* …? *Does she have to* …? Nevis *Do I must, Have I to* vai *Has she to.*

task: Put the words in order.
correct answer: i had to cancel my dentist appointment because i was stuck at work
wrong options / checks: also accepted: because i was stuck at work i had to cancel my dentist appointment
explanation shown to learner: For the past use *had to*: *I had to cancel …*. *must* has no past form for obligation.
explanation in Latvian: Pagātnē lieto *had to*: *I had to cancel* …. Pienākumam *must* pagātnes formas nav.

task: Put the words in order.
correct answer: i'll have to renew my passport before we fly to canada
wrong options / checks: also accepted: before we fly to canada i'll have to renew my passport
explanation shown to learner: *must* cannot follow *will*: use *will have to* (*we'll have to buy a new one*).
explanation in Latvian: Aiz *will* nevar likt *must*: lieto *will have to* (*we'll have to buy a new one*).

task: Put the words in order.
correct answer: we're going to have to hire more staff if sales keep growing
wrong options / checks: also accepted: if sales keep growing we're going to have to hire more staff
explanation shown to learner: *must* never follows another verb such as *might*, *will* or *going to*: use *have to* (*we might have to find …*, *we're going to have to …*).
explanation in Latvian: *must* nekad neliek aiz cita darbības vārda, piemēram, *might, will* vai *going to*: lieto *have to* (*we might have to find* …, *we're going to have to* …).

task: We ___ find a hotel near the station because the last train had already left.
correct answer: had to
wrong options / checks: bank: had to | must | have to
explanation shown to learner: For the past use *had to*: the last train had already left. *must* and *have to* are not past forms.
explanation in Latvian: Pagātnē lieto *had to*: pēdējais vilciens jau bija aizgājis. *must* un *have to* nav pagātnes formas.

task: If nobody can fix the printer today, we ___ ___ buy a new one.
correct answer: will / have to
wrong options / checks: bank: will | have to | must
explanation shown to learner: *must* cannot follow *will*: use *will have to* (*we'll have to buy a new one*).
explanation in Latvian: Aiz *will* nevar likt *must*: lieto *will have to* (*we'll have to buy a new one*).

task: ___ she ___ take the whole exam again if she fails one part?
correct answer: Does / have to
wrong options / checks: bank: Does | have to | Has | must
explanation shown to learner: Questions with *have to* use *do / does*: *Do I have to …? Does she have to …?* Not *Do I must*, *Have I to* or *Has she to*.
explanation in Latvian: Jautājumos ar *have to* lieto *do / does*: *Do I have to* …? *Does she have to* …? Nevis *Do I must, Have I to* vai *Has she to.*

task: The gym membership includes all the classes, so you ___ pay extra for yoga.
correct answer: don't have to
wrong options / checks: bank: don't have to | mustn't | don't must
explanation shown to learner: *don't have to* = it is not necessary: the classes are included. *mustn't* would mean it is not allowed.
explanation in Latvian: *don't have to* = nav vajadzības: nodarbības jau ir iekļautas. *mustn't* nozīmētu 'nedrīkst'. Tulkojot burtiski, 'nav jā…' šķiet *must not*, bet *mustn't* ir 'nedrīkst'.

task: Match each sentence with its meaning.
correct answer: I must book the tickets. = I feel it's necessary. ; I had to book the tickets. = It was necessary in the past. ; I don't have to book the tickets. = It isn't necessary. ; Do I have to book the tickets? = I'm asking if it's necessary.
explanation shown to learner: *must* = I feel it is necessary; *had to* = it was necessary; *don't have to* = it is not necessary; *Do I have to …?* asks if it is necessary.
explanation in Latvian: *must* = es jūtu, ka tas ir vajadzīgs; *had to* = tas bija vajadzīgs; *don't have to* = nav vajadzības; *Do I have to* …? jautā, vai tas ir vajadzīgs.

task: I couldn't park near the office, so I ___ leave the car three streets away. (have to)
correct answer: had to
explanation shown to learner: *couldn't* shows the past, so *had to*: *must* has no past form for obligation.
explanation in Latvian: *couldn't* rāda pagātni, tāpēc *had to*: pienākumam *must* pagātnes formas nav.

task: We ___ queue for long at the concert because we had bought our tickets online. (have to / not)
correct answer: didn't have to | did not have to
explanation shown to learner: Past negative: *didn't have to* = it was not necessary: *We didn't have to queue.*
explanation in Latvian: Noliegums pagātnē: *didn't have to* = nebija vajadzības: *We didn't have to queue.*

task: My sister works as a pilot, so she ___ have a medical check every year. (have to)
correct answer: has to | must | has got to | 's got to
explanation shown to learner: With *he / she / it* use *has to*: *she has to have a medical check*. *must* is correct too and does not change.
explanation in Latvian: Ar *he / she / it* lieto *has to*: *she has to have a medical check*. Der arī *must*, un tas nemainās.

task: ___ you ___ show your passport when you crossed the border last weekend? (have to)
correct answer: Did / have to
explanation shown to learner: Past question: *Did* + subject + *have to*: *Did you have to show your passport?* After *did* the verb is *have*, not *had*.
explanation in Latvian: Jautājums pagātnē: *Did* + teik. priekšmets + *have to*: *Did you have to show your passport?* Aiz *did* ir *have*, nevis *had*.

task: My flatmate ___ get up early on Mondays because her first class starts at eleven. (have to / not)
correct answer: doesn't have to | does not have to | hasn't got to | has not got to
explanation shown to learner: *doesn't have to* = it is not necessary: her class starts late. With *she* use *doesn't*.
explanation in Latvian: *doesn't have to* = nav vajadzības: viņas nodarbība sākas vēlu. Ar *she* lieto *doesn't*.

task: Start with *Last month*: I have to work every Saturday to cover for a sick colleague.
correct answer: Last month I had to work every Saturday to cover for a sick colleague.
explanation shown to learner: *Last month* is the past: *I had to work*. *must* has no past form for obligation.
explanation in Latvian: *Last month* ir pagātne: *I had to work.* Pienākumam *must* pagātnes formas nav.

task: Make a yes/no question: Anna has to take the medicine twice a day while she is ill.
correct answer: Does Anna have to take the medicine twice a day while she is ill? | Must Anna take the medicine twice a day while she is ill? | Has Anna got to take the medicine twice a day while she is ill? | Does Anna have to take the medicine twice a day?
explanation shown to learner: Question: *Does* + subject + *have to*: *Does Anna have to take …?* (*Must Anna take …?* is correct too, but formal.) Not *Has Anna to* or *Does Anna has to*.
explanation in Latvian: Jautājums: *Does* + teik. priekšmets + *have to*: *Does Anna have to take* …? (Der arī *Must Anna take* …?, bet tas ir oficiālāk.) Nevis *Has Anna to* vai *Does Anna has to.*

task: Say it another way with *might*: Perhaps we will have to sleep at the airport if the strike continues.
correct answer: We might have to sleep at the airport if the strike continues. | If the strike continues, we might have to sleep at the airport. | Perhaps we might have to sleep at the airport if the strike continues. | We might need to sleep at the airport if the strike continues. | If the strike continues, we might need to sleep at the airport.
explanation shown to learner: *might* + *have to*: *We might have to sleep …*. *will* goes; *must* cannot follow *might*.
explanation in Latvian: *might + have to*: *We might have to sleep* …. *will* izpaliek; aiz *might* nevar likt *must*.
